Summary  
Data-source overview: The post argues that current dietary choices in the effective-altruist / AI-safety community influence the long-term trajectory of factory farming and, therefore, the scope of animal suffering. It claims that AI technologies may entrench or scale factory farming and that AI alignment work that ignores non-human interests is a major risk. The author proposes value-shaping interventions—especially promoting ethical veganism among AI researchers—and technical / governance interventions that place animal welfare explicitly into AI objectives and data pipelines.

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[81]  
The extracted fabric follows the required category flow from three top-level risks through problem analyses, theoretical insights, design rationales, implementation mechanisms and validation evidence, ending in four distinct interventions. All nodes inter-connect; no intervention is directly linked to a risk; framework names are decomposed.  
Possible prompt improvement: allow an “contextualised_by” edge type so theoretical insights that merely size the stakes (e.g. tiny probabilities × huge scope) can be attached more naturally to risk/problem nodes.

Inference strategy justification  
Where the post provided only qualitative claims (e.g. “AI will increase stocking density”) I treated them as preliminary analyses (edge confidence 2). For one implementation detail (“historical proxy-gaming harms”) moderate inference (confidence 1) was required to create a complete path to an intervention on welfare-metric learning.

Extraction completeness explanation  
All arguments regarding (1) long-term factory-farming risk, (2) AI value alignment excluding animals, (3) AI technology reinforcing factory farming, (4) diet-shaped value signalling, and (5) dataset speciesism are represented. Each claim that drives the author’s reasoning appears as a separate node; every node is tied into at least one causal-interventional pathway.

Key limitations  
• Empirical evidence in the post is sparse; many validation nodes rest on single studies or forecasts, reflected in low-medium confidence scores.  
• Interventions are high-level; detailed technical specifications would require separate sources.  
• Some edges (e.g. TI1→DR1) rely on conceptual rather than causal enablement; more precise edge taxonomies could improve fidelity.
